newsitem.title: USA: White House's Stiglitz upbeat on consumer outlays.
newsitem.headline: White House's Stiglitz upbeat on consumer outlays.

text.p: White House chief economist Joseph Stiglitz on Monday forecast strong consumer spending in the fourth quarter and voiced optimism about the outlook for next year.

Speaking to reporters following a speech to the American Enterprise Institute, Stiglitz ticked off several reasons for optimism about the outlook for consumer outlays -- consumer confidence is high, real disposable income is rising and individual net worth is up.
"We have confidence that in the fourth quarter it's (consumer spending) going to be strong," he said.

Stiglitz declined comment on remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan last week. Greenspan rattled global financial markets after he raised the question about whether the U.S. stock market is overvalued.
However, Stiglitz, who heads the White House's Council of Economic Advisers, seemed to downplay the impact of last week's stock market slide on the economy.
"That was only a change in the stock market -- which is only a part of net worth -- of only one percent," he said.
Stiglitz also seemed to brush aside worries that recent wage increases could lead to higher inflation.

The Labor Department reported on Friday that average hourly earnings rose nine cents an hour in November. Stiglitz called those numbers "very volatile" and said the rise did not represent an inflationary trend.
He said he had no real concerns about the inflation outlook for next year. Corporate profit margins are very high so that companies have room to absorb "a bit faster" wage growth, he said.

The Labor Department also reported on Friday that the unemployment rate rose to 5.4 percent in November from 5.2 percent in October as jobs growth slowed to 118,000 from 224,000. Stiglitz said that the recent slowdown in jobs growth had been expected.
"The kinds of numbers that we're seeing are the kinds of numbers that we should expect to see over the future," he said.
That would mean that the unemployment rate would remain roughly around recent levels of 5.2 to 5.5 percent and monthly jobs growth would be in the 100,000 to 150,000 range, he said.
